title: Put ikke in basic sentences
goal: Place ikke correctly in simple Bokmål statements and questions.

objectives.statement: Place ikke correctly in simple Bokmål statements and questions.

spans.value: Maja and Elias work in the same office. They are deciding when to go for lunch.
Skal du ikke spise med oss?

blocks.translation: Aren’t you going to eat with us?

spans.value: Jo, men jeg har ikke matpakke i dag.

blocks.translation: Yes, but I don’t have a packed lunch today.

spans.value: Kjøper du ikke noe i kantina?

blocks.translation: Aren’t you buying anything in the cafeteria?

spans.value: Nei, den åpner ikke før elleve.

blocks.translation: No, it doesn’t open until eleven.

spans.value: Da går vi ikke ennå. Vi venter til elleve.

blocks.translation: Then we aren’t going yet. We’ll wait until eleven.

spans.value: The practical problem is simple: Elias wants lunch, but he has no packed lunch and the cafeteria is still closed. Maja and Elias use
several times to say that something is not true or to ask about a negative situation.
Useful expressions from the scene include:

en.value: I don’t have a packed lunch.

spans.value: A simple positive statement gives information:

spans.value: The verb that carries the tense is called the
is the finite verb. In a basic statement beginning with the subject, the order is:

en.value: Maja doesn’t eat in the cafeteria.

A common mistake is to copy English word order too closely:

A statement does not always begin with the subject. A time expression such as
can come first. The finite verb still keeps its normal main-clause position, and the subject follows it.

sections.title: Yes–no questions with a pronoun subject

spans.value: A yes–no question has no question word. It begins with the finite verb:
To make this a negative question, put
finite verb + pronoun subject + ikke + rest
This is the pattern heard in the dialogue:

en.value: Doesn’t he have a packed lunch?
Aren’t you going to leave soon?

spans.value: still follows the finite verb and pronoun subject:
A frequent mistake is to use statement order in a question:

en.value: Intended basic question: Aren’t you eating with us?

spans.value: That order can occur with special conversational intonation, but it is not the basic question pattern taught here. For a standard yes–no question, begin with the finite verb:

finite verb + ikke + full noun subject + rest

spans.value: This contrast is about subject form, not about the meaning of

spans.value: At eleven, Maja and Elias check the cafeteria again.
Nå er kantina åpen. Kommer du ikke?

blocks.translation: Now the cafeteria is open. Aren’t you coming?

spans.value: Jo, jeg kommer. Men jeg kjøper ikke varm mat.

blocks.translation: Yes, I’m coming. But I’m not buying hot food.

spans.value: Spiser du ikke varm mat til lunsj?

blocks.translation: Don’t you eat hot food for lunch?

spans.value: Nei, jeg gjør ikke det i dag.

blocks.translation: No, I’m not doing that today.

spans.value: Hvorfor kjøper du ikke et rundstykke?

blocks.translation: Why don’t you buy a bread roll?

spans.value: God idé. Da trenger jeg ikke å vente mer.

blocks.translation: Good idea. Then I don’t need to wait any longer.

prompt.value: Write four natural Norwegian lines about Maja and Elias. Include a subject-first negative statement with Jeg, a neutral negative question with pronoun subject du, a neutral negative question with full-noun subject Maja, and a negative modal statement beginning with Vi kan. Use ikke in each line. After each line, briefly identify its sentence type and subject form in Norwegian.

prompt.value: Write a short four-line exchange in natural Bokmål about Maja and Elias making plans after work. Include: a subject-first negative statement saying that Elias cannot come; a negative statement beginning with the time expression I kveld, saying that the shop is not open; a neutral yes-no negative question with pronoun subject du, asking whether du will go to the shop; and a neutral negative question with full-noun subject Maja, asking whether Maja is coming to the shop. The exchange should show that one person is unavailable, the shop is closed, and the original plan changes. Use ikke and your own wording.
